questions.text: Who or what actually runs the rollout controller, and what does a person do to advance a mode (button, command, approval)? Who is allowed to?
questions.about: person advances / Rollout controller's durable record

questions.text: In 'both' the old engine computes into the shadow store and the new engine writes the ledger. In 'shadow' invoices from both engines are compared, but in 'both' which two sets of invoices does the nightly job compare, given only the new engine charges?
questions.about: What each mode does / nightly job

questions.text: How exactly do workers stop charging in RB1? Is it a check of the controller record before each charge, and what happens to a charge request that arrives during the hold: queued, dropped, or delayed?
What does 'in-flight charges are allowed to settle' mean in practice? How long do you wait, and what if one never settles?
questions.about: RB1 -> RB2: charging held, in-flight charges settled

questions.text: In RB2, what is 'due but not made'? How does the system know which periods are due and who decides the list is complete?
If rollback is retried from RB2 after RB3 or RB4 partly ran, how does it avoid reprocessing events or double-charging? What makes the steps idempotent?
questions.about: RB_blocked -> RB2: on-call retries, rerun from reconcile

questions.text: Who or what starts the automatic rollback: what measures the 2% failure rate, and what counts as a charge failure (declined card vs. system error)?
questions.about: charge failures above 2 percent in 10 minutes

questions.text: In 'shadow' and 'both' the old and new engines both exist, but the 'both' to 'new_only' step stops the old engine. What exactly happens to the old engine and in-progress billing at that switch, and how does the 'billing_mode' flag change get to all workers consistently?
questions.about: both --> new_only / billing_mode flag in the config service

answers.text: The rollout controller is a service that holds the rollout record, checks gates and sets the flag. A person advances by sending an advance command to it, and it refuses if the gate is unmet. Who is allowed to send it is not known. The brief only says a person makes forward moves. Added to the file and to open question 8.

In both, the job compares the new engine's ledger invoices with the old engine's shadow-store invoices. In shadow it compares the old engine's ledger invoices with the new engine's shadow-store invoices. Fixed in the file. This is the only reading that keeps the comparison running in both, as the brief requires.

Yes. The controller records a hold, and each worker checks that record before every charge. A charge request that arrives during the hold waits and is retried after the hold ends. It is not dropped. RB1 ends when all workers confirm the hold. I chose delay over drop so that no due charge is lost, as the brief requires.

The rollback does not wait for in-flight charges. RB2 looks up every period by customer and period key, so a charge that never settles shows up there as unknown and is resolved by asking the provider. This removes the need for a settle timeout. The remaining timeout is for worker confirmations in RB1, which I have no defensible value for. It is listed as open question 9.

A due charge is a billing period that has an invoice but no charge for that customer and period key in the ledger or at the provider. RB2 is complete when every period with an invoice has a known status, and the controller decides this by checking its own list. This is my design. The brief says only that due charges must not be dropped.

Retry restarts from RB2, which rebuilds the due list from the ledger and provider each time. So charges that RB4 already made are seen as charged and skipped, because of the customer and period key. RB3 writes invoices under customer and period key, so a rerun replaces the same invoice. The RB3 property is a requirement on the old engine, not something I verified. It is recorded under open question 7.

The controller measures the failure rate over a sliding 10-minute window from charge results and starts rollback itself. What counts as a failure is not known. It is unclear whether a declined card counts or only system and provider errors. Neither is a minimum charge volume defined. Both are in open question 2.

At both to new_only the old engine finishes the invoice run it is on and then stops computing. That is stated in the file. How a flag change reaches all workers consistently is not known. The brief does not say. The file relies on the charge key check to prevent a double charge by a worker with a stale value. The propagation mechanism is recorded in open question 8.

questions.text: When rolling back from both or new_only, which invoices make up the due list: the new engine's ledger invoices or the old engine's shadow-store invoices? If their totals differ, which amount does the old engine charge in RB4?
While the rollback is running from new_only, new usage events keep arriving. Who computes invoices for them between RB1 and the flag being set to old_only, and does RB3 pick them up?
What starts a charge in the first place? Is there a scheduled invoice run, and does it run per billing period for all customers at once, or continuously?
In RB4, in what order do the old engine's charges, the flag change, stopping the new engine, and clearing the hold happen? What if the new engine has a charge in progress when it is stopped?
At the moment of the switch from shadow to both, how does charging hand over from the old engine to the new one for a period that is partly billed? Which period does the new engine charge first?
questions.about: shadow to both: person advances, 7 day gate met

questions.text: Are the 14 days in both consecutive, or a total count? What happens to the count when a day is unverified because the nightly comparison failed?
What happens if the rollout controller itself is down or slow, especially during a rollback hold? Do workers charge or wait when they cannot read the controller record?

answers.text: The due list is built from ledger invoices, because the ledger is the system of record. From both or new_only these are the new engine's invoices. The old engine charges the amount on the ledger invoice, not its own recomputed amount, so a differing shadow-store total never changes what is charged. RB3 only writes invoices for periods with no ledger invoice. Stated in RB2, RB3, RB4 and under the rollback table.

RB1 also stops the new engine starting new invoice runs, and usage events wait in the log. RB3 (from new_only) reads skipped events up to the present. Anything arriving after that is handled by the old engine's normal runs once the hold ends. I chose a full pause so the ledger does not change while the due list is being built.
The brief does not say what starts a charge or whether runs are scheduled per period or continuous. The plan only needs each charge to carry its customer and period key. Added as open question 10.

Order in RB4: stop the new engine, old engine charges the due list, set the flag to old_only, clear the hold and gate counters. The new engine is stopped first so it cannot start anything new. A charge it already had in progress is caught by the key check, and RB2 already looked up outcomes by key. Written into RB4.

Handover relies on the charge key. From the switch the new engine charges each period that has no charge for its key. A period the old engine already charged is skipped. No fixed first period is needed. Added to the shadow to both gate line.

The 14 days are a total, not necessarily consecutive, because the brief says 14 days in both with no unresolved mismatches, not consecutive. A day with a failed nightly comparison does not count toward the 14, so it delays the gate rather than resetting it. Unresolved mismatches must be zero when advancing. Stated in the gate line.

Fail closed. A worker that cannot read the controller record does not charge. Requests wait and are retried, so billing is delayed but never doubled. No forward move or automatic rollback happens while the controller is down. I chose this because a delayed charge is recoverable and a double charge is not. Added to the failure table.

questions.text: Workers check the hold record before every charge, and the hold is only cleared in RB4 step 4. How can the old engine charge the due list in RB4 step 2 while the hold is still on?

Between the new engine stopping (RB4 step 1) and the flag being set to old_only (step 3), what do workers see in billing_mode, and which engine acts on it? Is anything charging or computing in that gap?
questions.about: RB4 Resume: flag set to old_only

questions.text: If RB4 fails after the old engine has charged part of the due list but before the flag is set, what state is the system in while blocked? Is the new engine still stopped when the retry restarts from RB2?
Is the 35 days counted from entering new_only? If a rollback is already running when day 35 arrives, does the lock wait or does the rollback continue?
After the switch to new_only, who charges the periods from the old engine's last run, and how does the new engine know whether those periods are already charged?
questions.about: both --> new_only: At the switch the old engine finishes the invoice run it is on

answers.text: It cannot under the rule as written, so the rule was wrong. The hold now applies to normal charges only. The rollback's own charges in RB4 step 2 are exempt, and the hold is cleared in step 4. I chose this so due charges can be made while normal charging stays blocked. How a worker recognises a rollback charge is not decided and is open question 11.

Between RB4 step 1 and step 3 the flag still shows the starting mode (both or new_only). Nothing computes: the new engine is stopped and, under the hold, the old engine runs no invoice runs. The only charges are the rollback's own, made by the old engine in step 2. Added under the rollback table.

The system is blocked with the hold still on, the flag unchanged, and the new engine still stopped, because the controller records that the stop happened. Part of the due list may already be charged. The retry restarts from RB2, which sees those charges by key and skips them. Added to the failure table and to the controller record.

Yes, the 35 days are counted from entry into new_only, using the controller's recorded entry time. If a rollback already started before day 35, it continues to the end and the lock applies only if none is running. I chose this because locking mid-rollback would strand the system half rolled back. The brief does not say it, so it is flagged under open question 1.

The premise was mistaken. In both the old engine charges nothing, so its last run only writes to the shadow store and leaves no uncharged periods. The new engine has charged every period in both, with the key check preventing repeats. Reworded the both to new_only gate line to say this.

teachbacks.text:
1. The one setting that matters is the `billing_mode` flag, stored in the config service. It has four values, `old_only`, `shadow`, `both` and `new_only`, and workers read it. The rollout starts in `old_only`, where the old engine computes, charges and writes the ledger, and the new engine is off.

2. A person tells the rollout controller to advance. The controller checks the gate for the next mode and refuses if it isn't met. If the gate is met, it sets the flag and records the time of entry into the new mode in its durable record. A gate being met never moves the mode on its own, and only the next mode in order is allowed. The controller keeps the entry time because the 14-day and 35-day clocks need it.

3. `old_only` to `shadow` has no gate in the document. In `shadow` the old engine still does everything. The new engine reads the same usage events and writes invoices to the shadow store. It never charges and never writes the ledger. Errors from the new engine in this mode are recorded and never trigger a rollback.

4. Every night a comparison job runs in `shadow` and in `both`. It compares invoices per customer, between the ledger and the shadow store. A mismatch is a total that differs by more than one cent. The results are kept per day as gate evidence. A night when the job doesn't run or fails doesn't count, and that breaks the 7-day streak.

5. To go from `shadow` to `both`, the gate needs 7 consecutive days with a mismatch rate under 0.1%, and at least 5,000 invoices compared. A person advances and the controller sets the flag to `both`. From then on the new engine computes, charges and writes the ledger. The old engine keeps computing invoices into the shadow store but charges nothing. Before charging, each engine checks the customer plus billing period key against the ledger and the payment provider. A period the old engine already charged is skipped.

6. To go from `both` to `new_only`, the gate needs 14 days in `both` (a total, counting only days with a completed comparison). It also needs no unresolved mismatches and Finance sign-off. At the switch, the old engine finishes the shadow-store run it is on and then stops. In `new_only` the old engine skips usage events, and the new engine does everything.

7. Day 35 after entry into `new_only` is the lock. If no rollback is running on that day, the state becomes `new_only_locked`. The flag still reads `new_only`, and rollback is no longer possible. Failures are then fixed forward as incidents. The old engine may be decommissioned after that.

8. A rollback can start in `shadow`, `both` or `new_only`. On-call can start one by hand before the lock. The controller starts one automatically when the new engine's charge failure rate is above 2% over any 10-minute window, but only in `both` and `new_only`. A rollback already running ignores further triggers. A rollback started before day 35 runs to the end.

9. RB1 (Hold): the controller records a hold, along with the rollback id and starting mode, in its own record. Before each normal charge a worker checks that record. While the hold is on, charge requests wait and are retried afterwards, and none are dropped. The new engine starts no new invoice runs, and usage events pile up in the log. The step ends when every worker has confirmed the hold.

10. RB2 (Reconcile): in-flight charges are not waited for. For every billing period with a ledger invoice, the controller reads the ledger and asks the payment provider by customer and period key. Any charge with an unknown outcome, such as a timeout, is looked up this way and never blindly retried. When every period has a known status, the periods with a ledger invoice and no charge become the due list.

11. RB3 (Reprocess) runs only if the rollback started from `new_only`. The old engine reads the usage events it skipped and writes invoices to the ledger, only for periods that have no ledger invoice. Each is written under its customer and period key, so a rerun replaces the same invoice. From `both` or `shadow` this step is skipped and the flow goes straight to RB4.

12. RB4 (Resume) does four things in order. (1) The new engine is stopped and the controller records that. (2) The old engine charges the due list, using the amount on each ledger invoice. These charges are exempt from the hold. (3) The flag is set to `old_only`. (4) The hold and gate counters are cleared. Until step 3 the flag still shows the starting mode, but nothing computes and only the rollback's own charges happen. After the hold ends, the old engine's normal runs handle events that arrived later. The rollout then restarts at `shadow`, with the 7-day and 14-day counts starting over.

13. Failure of a rollback step: the rollback goes to "blocked" and on-call is paged. The hold stays on, the flag is unchanged, and the new engine stays stopped if RB4 had already stopped it. On-call retries and the run restarts from RB2. This is safe because RB2 rebuilds the due list from the ledger and provider, and RB3 and RB4 only act on periods with no ledger invoice or no charge for that key.

14. Other failures:
- Provider timeout on a charge: the outcome is unknown, so look it up by key before any retry.
- Config service unreachable: workers keep their last known mode and no forward move can be made.
- Controller unreachable: workers can't read the hold record, so they don't charge. Billing is delayed, never doubled, and no forward move or automatic rollback happens until it returns.
- Stale mode on a worker after a forward move: the key check stops a second charge for the same period.
gaps: How a flag change reaches all workers, and what a worker does with a charge it started under the old mode value (open question 8).
Who is allowed to send the advance command to the controller, and how it is sent or authenticated (open question 8).
What the gate for old_only to shadow is. The document gives none, so it is unclear whether a person can advance at any time.
What starts a charge, and whether invoice runs are scheduled per period or run continuously (open question 10). I can't say what triggers the step where a worker charges a due period.
How a worker tells a rollback charge in RB4 from a normal charge when the hold is on (open question 11).

How the controller counts the 2% failure rate, including a minimum number of charges per window and whether declined cards count (open question 2). The automatic trigger can't be fully explained without it.
How workers confirm the hold to the controller, and what happens if a worker never confirms. No timeout is set (open question 9).
What happens in RB3 when the usage events it needs have expired from the 35-day log, for a rollback started on day 33 or 34 (open question 1).
How the controller gets the comparison results and decides a mismatch is resolved. The document says only that a person closes it with a reason, as an assumption (open question 4).
Whether a missing new-engine invoice in shadow counts as a mismatch (open question 5).

How a worker enforces the key check against both the ledger and the provider in a single charge. The document gives the rule but not the mechanism, and says the rule is the author's own design requirement (open question 7).
What the controller's durable record is, such as its storage and how workers read it without making every charge depend on it.
